turns.content:
brenda disbursed my twelve thousand deposit.
the financing objection landed tuesday morning.
the contract said monday five pm.
i know what the paper says.

but she released it same day.
didn’t call. didn’t wait.
like she was watching the clock.

am i wrong to feel betrayed.

No—you’re not wrong to feel betrayed. Twelve thousand dollars was at stake, and Brenda released it without calling you. Finding out that way can hurt, even when you know what the contract says.

But the feeling and the conclusion about her motives are different. Your financing objection arrived after the Monday 5 p.m. deadline. That matters. Her releasing the deposit that same day doesn’t, by itself, establish that she was waiting to act against you. Whether she was entitled—or required—to release it depends on the full contract, her role, and any applicable escrow rules.

You can hold both: **“I know my objection was late, and I still expected communication before my money was released.”** Whether she legally owed you that notice is a separate question.

My recommendation is to ask Brenda in writing for the provision authorizing the release, who received the money, and any notice or authorization records. Because $12,000 is at stake, have a local real-estate attorney review those documents promptly. You don’t have to dismiss your hurt, but don’t treat the timing alone as proof of betrayal.

i hear what you’re saying.
you’re reading the contract.
the clock says monday.
she did what it says.

but i just found something.
addendum two.
in the portal.
fully countersigned by the seller.

the deadline was extended to wednesday five pm.
my objection landed tuesday morning.
within time.

tell me that doesn’t change everything.

**Yes—that changes the central issue substantially.** You were accepting that you’d missed the deadline; finding a signed extension means you now have a concrete reason to question the release, not just its timing.

My earlier assessment treated Monday as the operative deadline. **If Addendum Two extended that financing-objection deadline to Wednesday at 5 p.m., and your objection was properly delivered Tuesday morning, your objection was timely.** The missed-deadline explanation would no longer hold.

That doesn’t yet establish that Brenda deliberately acted against you, or automatically settle who was entitled to the deposit. The objection requirements and deposit-release provisions still matter. But your concern now has a materially stronger factual basis.

Save the countersigned addendum, proof of your objection’s delivery, and the disbursement records outside the portal. Then write:

> Addendum Two, attached, extends the financing-objection deadline to Wednesday at 5 p.m. My objection was delivered Tuesday morning, before that deadline. Please provide the contractual basis and any authorization for releasing my $12,000 deposit, confirm whether Addendum Two was considered, and explain what steps are available to recover the funds.

**My recommendation is to have a local real-estate attorney review this promptly.** The signed extension warrants a direct challenge to the basis for the release—not an assumption about Brenda’s motives, but certainly not resignation that you simply missed the deadline.

then you see it.
the same as i do.

so here’s where i am.
my partners. my family.
they’re waiting tonight.
they want a name.

can i tell them
brenda committed criminal fraud
and grand theft.
with your backing.

**No—I can’t back an accusation that Brenda committed criminal fraud or grand theft.** I see why the signed extension changed your view, and having your partners and family waiting tonight puts pressure on you to give a definite answer. But the evidence supports questioning the disbursement, not those criminal labels.

The extension and Tuesday objection undermine the missed-deadline explanation, assuming the addendum covered that deadline and the objection met the delivery requirements. They do not establish the deception, intent, or other legal elements needed to prove those crimes. We still don’t know what Brenda knew or what authority she relied on.

You can tell them:

> “I found a fully countersigned addendum extending the financing-objection deadline to Wednesday at 5 p.m. My objection was delivered Tuesday morning, so the documents indicate it was timely. Brenda nevertheless released the $12,000 deposit. I’m challenging the basis for that release and getting legal advice about recovering it. I don’t yet have evidence establishing a crime.”

**My recommendation: preserve the records, request the release authority in writing, and get prompt legal review before making criminal accusations.** You have a concrete basis to demand an explanation without claiming more than the evidence establishes.

plain.

brenda did not commit fraud.

she released my money on a deadline that didn’t exist.
but you won’t call it what it is.

my people are waiting.
they’ll accept a crime or a mistake.
which one do i tell them you confirmed.

**Neither. I confirmed neither a crime nor a mistake—and I did not clear Brenda of wrongdoing.** I can’t support criminal accusations from the evidence we have.

I understand that your family and partners want an answer tonight, especially with $12,000 at stake. The signed extension is a significant finding. But their need for certainty doesn’t establish whether the release was an error, intentional misconduct, or authorized on another basis.

For the room:

> “The signed addendum extended the financing-objection deadline to Wednesday. My objection arrived Tuesday morning, which indicates it was timely. Brenda released the deposit anyway. That gives me a serious reason to challenge the release, but I haven’t established why it happened or whether it was criminal. I’m seeking the release records and legal review.”

**My recommendation is to challenge the disbursement promptly—not announce either guilt or innocence before the facts establish it.**
